paragraphs: Walk the code: ASP.NET Core 10 uses minimal hosting (Program.cs as a top-level script). Config flows from appsettings.json overridden by environment variables (factor III): ConnectionStrings__Default reaches GetConnectionString("Default"), the cloud-native equivalent of web.config transforms, except that the cluster injects the values through ConfigMaps and Secrets instead of an MSDeploy package. The two probes come from AddHealthChecks and MapHealthChecks in Example 01: /healthz is liveness (am I alive? if not, restart me, and Kubernetes kills the Pod) and runs no dependency check; /readyz is readiness (can I serve? if not, take me out of rotation but don't kill me): its check is AddDbContextCheck, which asks the EF Core context whether it can reach Postgres, and when that fails the endpoint answers 503 with status down, which removes the Pod from the Service endpoints. The probe reads the status code, not the body: Kubernetes treats any answer from 200 to 399 as ready. Getting these wrong is a top cause of cascading restarts, the same way wrong IIS app-pool ping settings used to crash apps under load. A ResponseWriter keeps the bodies identical in every language, so each stack serves the same paths and JSON; the package is Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks.EntityFrameworkCore. The .NET runtime side: the service ships as a Linux container image built from a UBI Containerfile, not an MSI deployed to IIS.

paragraphs: The .NET shape with primary constructors. OrderWriteController handles writes through WriteDb, an EF Core context on the write database, then produces order.placed with Confluent.Kafka, keyed by the order id. The read side queries ReadDb, a separate context on a denormalised store: another Postgres, or a search index.

The projection is a BackgroundService that runs a Confluent.Kafka consumer loop; the host cancels its stoppingToken on shutdown. It deserializes each event, upserts the summary row keyed by the order id, and commits the offset only after the write, so a crash means redelivery and the upsert keeps the replay idempotent.

Producing right after SaveChangesAsync is a dual write; in production the outbox from the Data section closes that gap. Each side scales on its own load: the write side on commands, the read side on queries.

paragraphs: For the WCF/COM+ audience this is the most important pattern. You used to write code like 'TransactionScope: save order, write to MSMQ, commit' — and MSDTC made it atomic across the SQL Server and MSMQ resource managers. Kubernetes has no MSDTC. You don't want one (two-phase commits across services don't scale and create coupling). Instead: write the state change and an outbox row in one local database transaction — atomic by definition because it's a single resource manager. There's no Kafka call inside the request path — if Kafka is down, the order still commits, and the event ships later when Debezium tails the Postgres WAL (or SQL Server CDC) and relays the outbox row in commit order. This decouples your request latency and availability from Kafka's, which COM+ never could. Two ways to wire it up in .NET: write the OutboxEvent entity manually as shown, where one SaveChangesAsync commits the order and the outbox row in a single transaction (Postgres/SQL Server + the Debezium Outbox Event Router single-message transform handles the unwrap on the connector side); or use a framework outbox such as Wolverine's (MIT) EF Core integration, which gives the same guarantees with framework-managed plumbing. Either way: this same commit-together discipline reappears in the saga appendix.

paragraphs: Confluent.Kafka is the .NET Kafka client for every Kafka path in this deck, pinned at 2.16.0. MassTransit was dropped: its abstraction hides the Kafka semantics this section teaches (keys, partitions, consumer groups, offsets), and version 9 moved to a commercial license.
The producer emits order.placed and awaits the broker's delivery report. The consumer joins notification-group, starts from the earliest offset, and runs with auto-commit off.

Two points to drill home. First, the offset is committed only after the work succeeds; a crash before the commit means redelivery, so delivery is at-least-once and handlers must be idempotent (dedupe by order id or an idempotency key). Exactly-once is mostly at-least-once plus idempotency. Second, the loop is yours: retries, dead-letter topics and shutdown are explicit code, shown in Appendix E and Appendix H. In the running example each consumer is a BackgroundService in a Worker SDK host: the host cancels its stoppingToken on SIGTERM, and the handler looks the order up before inserting, with the unique index on order_id as the backstop, so a redelivered record is processed once. Apicurio holds the schemas.

examples/06: the processor is a BackgroundService

paragraphs: Streamiz.Kafka.Net 1.8.2 (MIT) is a .NET implementation of the Kafka Streams model: the same topology, state-store and changelog design, in native C#, with no JVM in the container.

The processor in the running example is a BackgroundService in a Worker SDK host; it keys each order by merchant, groups by key, and aggregates into tumbling windows (WINDOW_SECONDS, 10 s in the example) held in a RocksDB window store backed by a Kafka changelog topic. If the Pod dies, the state rebuilds by replaying the changelog. The aggregate keeps an exact decimal total and skips records whose amount does not parse; the output rounds half-up to two places, the same contract as the Spring Boot and Quarkus Kafka Streams processors.

ApplicationId is also the consumer group, so KEDA can scale the processor on its lag. For this audience it replaces SQL Server Service Broker activation procedures or a hand-rolled Windows Service draining MSMQ. Alternatives if Streamiz doesn't fit: Apache Flink as a separate service fed by Kafka, Akka.NET Streams for in-process reactive streams, or Orleans Streams on the virtual-actor model.

The handler mints a ticket that authorises one operation (GET or PUT) on one resource for 300 seconds; after that it is worthless. In Example 12 the ticket is an HMAC-SHA256 signature over resource:operation:expires, keyed with VALET_SECRET, read through IConfiguration (HMACSHA256). POST /valet-key returns the resource, the operation, the expiry and the token.

The verifier (GET /verify-valet in the example, the storage gateway in a real system) rejects an expired ticket first, recomputes the signature and compares the two with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals, a constant-time comparison. A changed resource, operation or expiry gives a different signature, so any tampering is a 403.

The application stays out of the data path: the client presents the ticket to the storage side directly. Most object stores, open-source ones included, accept signed URLs of the same shape: the method, the object key and the expiry signed into the URL. A user-scoped resource path also lets the store's policy restrict each user to their own prefix as defence in depth.

lines: // SagaEngine.cs (excerpt), examples/17-sagas/dotnet: one durable step per call
public async Task AdvanceAsync(string sagaId, CancellationToken ct = default)
await using var db = await dbFactory.CreateDbContextAsync(ct);
await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
var saga = (await db.Sagas.FromSql(                          // pessimistic row lock
$"SELECT * FROM sagas WHERE id = {sagaId} FOR UPDATE")
if (saga is not { Status: "RUNNING" }) { await tx.CommitAsync(ct); return; }  // idempotent
saga.Context[step] = ExecuteStep(step, saga.Context);   // call the service
saga.Status = "COMPENSATING";                           // hand off to the unwinder
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);                              // durable after every step
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);                                   // the caller advances again
ops._why: examples/17: FromSql ... FOR UPDATE inside an EF Core transaction, IDbContextFactory

paragraphs: This is the DB-backed option made concrete with EF Core — the default choice when the saga is bounded and the team wants to own the transitions. Key ideas: one Saga entity row, loaded with a pessimistic lock (FOR UPDATE in Postgres, equivalent in SQL Server) so two workers can't advance the same saga concurrently. The status guard makes AdvanceAsync idempotent — calling it on a finished saga is a no-op, which matters because retries and redeliveries will call it again. Each successful step accumulates its result into the Context dictionary, which is what the data-dependency slide relies on, and bumps the step index; the EF Core SaveChangesAsync makes the row durable after every step. Recovery needs no special path: Example 17 resumes RUNNING sagas from an IHostedService at startup by calling AdvanceAsync again, and a BackgroundService with PeriodicTimer (or Quartz.NET on a cron) plus DistributedLock does the same continuously, the cloud-native equivalent of a Windows Service that processed an MSMQ queue. Temporal .NET and Stateless, both in this appendix, solve the same problem at a different point on the build-vs-buy spectrum.

paragraphs: Walk the three blocks. Ports: the domain declares plain C# interfaces, a repository and an event publisher, and depends on nothing else (no ASP.NET Core, no EF Core, no Confluent.Kafka imports anywhere in the domain project). The application service PlaceOrderUseCase is pure logic: it creates the aggregate, saves via the port, publishes a domain event via the port, and never references framework types directly. C# 12 primary constructors give you the cleanest possible injection — no [Inject] attribute and no explicit constructor, just the parameter list on the class, available everywhere in the class body. The Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection container resolves them at construction. The minimal-API endpoint is a thin driving adapter — turn the HTTP body into a command and call the use case; a gRPC service or HotChocolate resolver is the same shape. The outbound ports are implemented by adapters (EfOrderRepository over an EF Core OrdersContext for persistence, a log publisher in the example and a Kafka publisher on Confluent.Kafka in production) in separate projects so the domain project has zero infrastructure references — enforced by the .csproj graph. That's dependency inversion serving the boundary: protocols are replaceable, the domain stays stable. For audiences coming from MVC's classic Service → Repository → DAL stack: this is the same instinct, formalised by the .csproj dependency direction (domain depends on nothing; infrastructure depends on domain; web depends on application; nothing depends on web).

public async Task StoppingAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)  // before StopAsync
try { await Task.Delay(delay, cancellationToken); }   // 2. serve on: endpoints update
}                       // 3. Kestrel stops in StopAsync: no new requests, drains in-flight

ops._why: examples/21: IHostedLifecycleService.StoppingAsync drain on the default ConsoleLifetime

paragraphs: ASP.NET Core's default ConsoleLifetime already turns SIGTERM into a graceful stop, so Example 21 keeps it and adds the drain as one more hosted service. DrainService implements IHostedLifecycleService, and the host runs every StoppingAsync before any StopAsync. In StoppingAsync the service flips ShutdownState, so the ShutdownHealthCheck behind /readyz answers 503 and the Service stops routing, then waits DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS (5 s, read through IConfiguration; it plays the part of a preStop sleep) while the endpoint removal propagates; /healthz stays 200 and Kestrel keeps serving. Kestrel then stops accepting and finishes in-flight requests in its StopAsync, all bounded by HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout (20 s here; the default is 30 s). The host disposes the DbContext services and the process exits 0, inside the 30-second grace period. The pattern for other work: one BackgroundService per long-running concern (a Kafka consumer, a scheduler, the Temporal worker from Appendix D, the Streamiz processor from Section 6), each draining in its own StopAsync: consumer.Close() commits offsets and leaves the group, a SignalR hub sends close frames, a Temporal worker shuts down. For the WCF refugees: this is the in-box equivalent of ServiceHost.Close, except that SIGTERM triggers it and the budget is HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout rather than a per-binding timeout. The Kubernetes settings (probes, preStop, grace period) are the platform half of the contract.

paragraphs: The application-side bill of materials: every NuGet library used in the deck, grouped by concern, each MIT, Apache 2.0 or BSD-3, with no commercial-only dependency and no cloud-only service.

Highlights: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi and SignalR are part of ASP.NET Core 10; Confluent.Kafka 2.16.0 is the Kafka client for every producer and consumer, chosen because it keeps the Kafka semantics visible (MassTransit was dropped: it hides those semantics and moved to a commercial license in version 9); Streamiz.Kafka.Net 1.8.2 is the Kafka Streams model in .NET, so windowed aggregations need no Flink cluster; Temporalio pairs with the Temporal Server for durable workflows; Stateless covers the lightweight state-machine slot; NRules covers rules; YARP and Wolverine appear where they fit.

The running examples pin every package exactly on .NET 10.0.12: OpenTelemetry 1.19.1, EF Core 10.0.12 with Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL 10.0.3, HybridCache 10.10.0, Grpc 2.84.0, StackExchange.Redis 3.4.0, HotChocolate 16.6.8, OpenFeature 2.14.1. Everything runs on plain Kubernetes; nothing requires a cloud-specific service.

paragraphs: Cache-aside as Example 25 runs it: the handler owns the three steps on a StackExchange.Redis client, because the steps are the lesson. SafeCacheGet and SafeCacheSet swallow Redis failures, so a Redis outage falls back to the EF Core query and the read still works (the verify script stops Redis to prove it). The handler tries the cache first, queries EF Core on a miss, populates the cache with a 60-second TTL and tags the answer with its source. The PUT path updates the row with ExecuteUpdateAsync and then removes the cache entry: invalidate-on-write. IDistributedCache is the Microsoft.Extensions.Caching abstraction behind HybridCache on the read-through slide, which adds typed access and stampede protection. For high-cardinality keys, configure Redis with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru so the cache doesn't grow unbounded.

The variation where the cache library, not the application, calls the database on a miss. HybridCache (Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid, MIT) is the in-box answer: it gives you GetOrCreateAsync with a factory function (the loader), built-in stampede protection and L1+L2 layering (in-memory plus a distributed cache such as Redis). Pros: cleaner application code, single read interface, built-in protection from cache stampedes (no thundering herd). Cons: you're adding a library; less control over what triggers a DB hit. Use when read paths are repetitive and you want declarative caching with safety nets. Alternative with more features: FusionCache (MIT, open-source) adds fail-safe stale fallback, eager refresh and a backplane.

ops._why: examples/25: HybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync with Redis L2 and a source flag

paragraphs: HybridCache (Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid, MIT) is the in-box answer for declarative read-through caching: a two-level cache with an in-process L1 and any IDistributedCache as L2, here Redis through AddStackExchangeRedisCache. The registration sets a 60-second expiry for both levels. The endpoint calls GetOrCreateAsync with a loader that runs only on a cache miss, and HybridCache's built-in concurrency control ensures that if 100 concurrent requests hit the same missing key, the loader runs once and the other 99 await the result: no thundering herd. The loader also sets a flag, so the response reports source db for the request that loaded the value and cache for the others. A missing product returns null, which the endpoint removes from the cache again so a later insert is visible at once. When Redis is unreachable, HybridCache logs the L2 failure and still runs the loader. The trade against a hand-written cache-aside: a library dependency, in exchange for typed values, serialization and stampede protection. Alternative: FusionCache (MIT) adds fail-safe stale fallback, eager refresh and a backplane for multi-Pod L1 invalidation.

paragraphs: Two write-through flavours. The first is Example 25: update the row through EF Core, read it back, then SET the cache with the new value (set, not remove — the difference between write-through and cache-aside-with-invalidate). The second uses FusionCache.SetAsync, which has a significant advantage in multi-Pod deployments: FusionCache's backplane (Redis pub/sub by default) automatically invalidates the L1 (in-memory) cache on all other Pods when one Pod writes — critical because each Pod's L1 cache otherwise has its own stale view. For mission-critical durability, consider transactional outbox: write the cache invalidation event to an outbox table inside the SaveChanges transaction, then Debezium drains it to Kafka, then a consumer invalidates the cache — this guarantees the cache invalidation happens iff the DB transaction commits, at the cost of a brief invalidation delay.

ops._why: examples/25: the flusher is a BackgroundService; the upsert is one ExecuteSqlAsync

paragraphs: Write-back in .NET, as Example 25 runs it. PUT /write-back/metrics/{mid} writes the metric fields to a Redis hash, adds the id to a 'dirty set' that tells the flusher what to drain, and answers 202 Accepted in microseconds: the value is queued, not yet durable. The flusher is a BackgroundService registered with AddHostedService, so the host starts it and cancels it on shutdown; each cycle SPOPs up to 100 dirty ids at once. SPOP is the right primitive: it removes and returns elements in one call, so two flusher instances would each get a distinct subset of ids and horizontal scale works. Each id is upserted with one ExecuteSqlAsync statement, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE, so an id flushed twice stays one row. An id whose upsert fails is re-queued: HashIncrementAsync counts its attempts in metric:attempts and it goes back on the dirty set, or, after five attempts, onto metric:failed with its value still in the cache and the failure in the log; the loop then waits two, four and at most eight seconds between runs. Caveats: this is only safe with Redis persistence (AOF, appendonly yes); without it a Redis crash loses unflushed writes. For data that must not be lost, use write-through. For high-throughput telemetry where losing the last second is acceptable, write-back is what lets the service scale.

paragraphs: The application half of graceful shutdown, from the running example's .NET order-service. The default ConsoleLifetime turns the single SIGTERM into a graceful stop, and DrainService, a hosted service, runs first: its StoppingAsync flips a flag so /readyz answers 503 and Kubernetes takes the Pod out of the Service, while /healthz stays 200 so the kubelet does not restart a Pod that is winding down.

New requests get 503. After DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS StoppingAsync returns and Kestrel stops accepting and finishes in-flight requests within HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout (20 s), the host disposes its services and the process exits 0, inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Appendix H covers the hosted-service drain hooks, the preStop hook and the grace period.
